Abstract
A high frequency pairs trading (HFPT) algorithm is built by the integration of pairs
trading and threshold rebalancing algorithm. The determination of optimal threshold
(OT) for the HFPT is crucial to maximize its proﬁtability, and this study suggests a
procedure to classify OT ranges by supervised machine learning (ML) techniques.
In this regard, a sample dataset is created for ML applications. In this dataset, the
target variables (OT values) are computed by the application of HFPT algorithm to
real price data of 50 crypto-assets, and input variables (features) are calculated as
portfolio mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, value at risk, and correlation coefﬁcient
of the pairs. Before classiﬁcation process, the pairs (or portfolios) are divided into
three sub-groups (as positively, weakly and negatively correlated), and then OT values
are classiﬁed by 6 ML methods. Comparing the evaluation metrics for ML methods, it
is observed that the best accuracy, precision and F1-scores are obtained by the Random
Forest (RF) classiﬁer for all portfolio groups in two-class, three-class and four-class
classiﬁcation. Also, it is seen that the right classiﬁcation performance of ML methods
on positively and negatively correlated pairs are better than weakly correlated pairs.
Furthermore, the success of RF classiﬁer is veriﬁed with a test dataset that contains
price series of 50 crypto-assets in January and February 2024. The applicability of
OT range classiﬁcation procedure in practical exchange markets is also demonstrated,
and it is shown that the HFPT algorithm can yield reasonable proﬁts when threshold
selected in predicted range.

1 Introduction
Research on pair-trading has a long tradition. As mentioned in prior literature, the
pair-trading strategy relies on the historical co-movement between the prices of two
securities. When two stock prices have shown a pattern of moving together, this trend
will probably persist in the future. Any deviation in prices is capitalized upon by open-
ing a long position in the undervalued security and a short position in the overvalued
one. Proﬁts are then made by closing these positions when the spread returns to its
historical equilibrium (Gatev et al., 2006). The pairs trading approach can be broken
down into three simple steps: Initially, a pair of stocks is selected, and then the mean
and the standard deviation of the price ratio between the two stocks are calculated.
Latter when the price ratio deviates from the mean by two standard deviations, the
strategy involves selling the overpriced stock and simultaneously buying the under-
priced one. Finally, as the price ratio reverts to the mean, positions are cleared to
realize proﬁts from the trade. It’s important to note that investors are not necessarily
bound to the rule of using two standard deviations as the trigger point in the second
step. Instead, they can strategically adjust this trigger point according to market con-
ditions and the actual movement of the pair. Likewise, there is no strict rule for closing
positions when the spread reverts to the mean. Investors might wait longer to realize
larger proﬁts potentially, but this decision also comes with increased risk (Zeng &
Lee, 2014).
In the past several decades, numerous quantitative methods have been developed
in the ﬁeld of pair-trading. A thorough review of the literature by Krauss (2017)
revealed that research on pair-trading strategies can be categorized into ﬁve distinct
approaches. The ﬁrst one is the metric approach which utilizes nonparametric distance
measurements to detect pair-trading opportunities. The remaining four methodologies
include the cointegration approach, the time series approach, the stochastic control
approach, and various other approaches such as the machine learning (ML) approach,
the copula approach, and the principal components analysis approach.

In the distance approach, several metrics have been proposed to screen and select
stocks, some focusing on the sum of Euclidean distance Gatev et al. (2006), while
others on Pearson correlation coefﬁcient Do and Faff (2010). Based on Engle and
Granger’s (1987) cointegration theory, Vidyamurthy (2004) proposed a three-step
framework for pair-trading. Initially, pairs are selected relying on statistical measures.
Then, the cointegration test is performed, and ﬁnally, optimal thresholds are deter-
mined using nonparametric methods. The cointegration relationship between the two
assets signiﬁes a long-term relationship. Taking advantage of this relationship, one can
effectively model the co-movement of an asset pair and use it to implement a high-
performance pair-trading strategy. The major beneﬁt of the cointegration approach
is that it provides long-term relationships between traded assets based on short-term
deviations from this long-run equilibrium with the expectation of mean reversion.
Lin et al. (2006) proposed a minimum proﬁt condition for a pair of securities that
exhibit cointegration over the relevant time horizon. While Lin et al. (2006) veri-
ﬁed the statistical validity of the procedure through simulation data, its practicality
was also tested using real data. The authors noted that at reasonable minimum proﬁt
levels, the protocol does not signiﬁcantly reduce trade numbers or absolute proﬁts
compared to an unprotected trading strategy. The cointegration method was further
applied by (Puspaningrum et al., 2010; Dunis et al., 2010; Gutierrez & Tse, 2011; Rad
et al., 2016).
The state space model performed by Elliott et al. (2005) is in the ﬁeld of the
time series approach. Elliott et al. (2005) expressed the spread as a mean-reverting
Gaussian Markov chain. One practical advantage of the model is that it can estimate
parameters. Do et al. (2006) have driven the further development of a pair-trading
methodology that models mispricing at the return instead of the price level. Once the
model has been effectively calibrated, a long-short position is initiated whenever the
accumulated spread over a speciﬁc period exceeds certain threshold values. However,
these thresholds and the expected holding duration were not explicitly deﬁned and
need to be assessed for potential implementation (Krauss, 2017). In these studies, an
Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process was employed to model the price spread between two
stocks. Research in the time-series approach either discusses theoretical frameworks
or concentrates on developing trading algorithms.
Jurek and Yang (2007) have attracted more attention in the ﬁeld of Stochastic
Control Approach. Their research focused on determining the best dynamic strategy
for non-myopic arbitrageurs who face a mean-reverting arbitrage opportunity. The
other group of papers has integrated neural networks for forecasting and multi-criteria
decision methods for the selection of pairs (Huck, 2009, 2010). Huck (2009) used
ELECTRE III, an outranking method based on fuzzy logic as a multi-criteria analysis
method. In addition, Krauss et al. (2017) examined the effectiveness of deep neural
networks, gradient-boosted trees, and random forests concerning statistical arbitrage.
Following there has been an extended use of the copula approach in pair trading
studies Liew and Wu (2013); Stander et al. (2013); Rad et al. (2016); Krauss and
Stübinger (2017). In their paper, Avellaneda and Lee (2010) studied model-driven sta-
tistical arbitrage in US equities by using Principal Component Analysis and regressing
stock returns on sector Exchange Traded Funds. The residuals or idiosyncratic returns
were modeled as mean-reverting processes in all these cases.

Although many studies have applied pairs trading to stock, exchange-traded funds,
and commodity markets, the research on cryptocurrency markets remains limited.
Besides traditional pairs trading methods, Ko et al. (2023) considered two evolution-
ary algorithms: genetic algorithm and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II to
examine the proﬁtability of pairs trading for 26 cryptocurrencies. Their results show
that the second algorithm has the highest return rates at high frequencies. Similarly,
Fil and Kristoufek (2020) have employed the distance and cointegration methods to
a basket of 26 liquid cryptocurrencies. They found evidence that pairs trading can
perform well in the cryptocurrency market with higher-frequency trading. They also
suggested that exogenous factors such as transaction costs or execution windows are
extremely important.
Over the past two decades, algorithmic trading (AT), characterized by computer
algorithms executing trades automatically, has experienced signiﬁcant growth with the
technological advancements (Chaboud et al., 2014; Cartea et al., 2015). It currently
accounts for up to 70 percent of overall trading volume in certain exchange mar-
kets (European Central Bank, 2019). AT involves the automatic execution of orders
using predeﬁned mathematical rules based on factors like price, time, and quantity,
often with minimal or no human intervention (Chaboud et al., 2014; Cartea et al.,
2018). AT can execute operations on markets at incredibly high speeds and frequencies
compared to manual trading. This phenomenon is often referred to as high-frequency
trading (HFT), as trade horizons are shortened to minutes, seconds, or even millisec-
onds (Cartea & Jaimungal, 2013; Vo & Yost-Bremm, 2020; Jain et al., 2021; Virgilio,
2022). The HFT is characterized by several key features, including high speeds, high
turnover rates, and high order-to-trade ratios. The execution of trading strategies in
HFT relies on sophisticated algorithms and advanced technological tools. Moreover,
with the rise of artiﬁcial intelligence and ML techniques, AT has become increasingly
popular among ﬁnancial traders (Konrad & Philip, 1994; Liu et al., 2021; Zhang et
al., 2021).
Portfolio rebalancing (PR) strategies have been widely adopted in the ﬁeld of
AT (DeMiguel et al., 2009; Zilinskij, 2015; Dayanandan & Lam, 2015; Ba˘gcı &
Kaya Soylu, 2024). PR ensures that the portfolio risk is aligned with the investor’s
objectives and risk preference. There are three common kinds of strategies for PR
that are periodic rebalancing, threshold rebalancing, and a combination of these two
strategies (Zilinskij, 2015; Zilbering et al., 2015). When the portfolio weights of assets
are rebalanced according to the desired asset allocation within a predetermined time
interval, it is called a periodic rebalancing strategy. In this strategy, the only variable
is the time (Das et al., 2014; Costabile & Gaudenzi, 2017), and the rebalancing period
may vary depending on the market volatility condition. If the ﬁnancial markets are
high volatile, the transaction period can be shortened.
The second strategy is threshold rebalancing, in which the allocation of assets in the
portfolio is rebalanced if the portfolio’s weights deviate from the target asset allocation
by more than a predetermined tolerance level (Bernoussi & Rockinger, 2022; Dai et al.,
2024; Ba˘gcı & Kaya Soylu, 2024). Determining this threshold may be based on various
factors, such as market-based indicators, models predicting returns, or risk assessments
(Moallemi & Saglam, 2015). The last one is periodic and threshold rebalancing strat-
egy, which is a combination of periodic and threshold strategies. In this approach,

To ensure maximum proﬁt over time in the long run, it is crucial for the investor

Previous researches used the RL framework to determine the optimal thresholds
(Fallahpour et al., 2016; Kim & Kim, 2019). Fallahpour et al. (2016) combined coin-
tegration approach with the RL method using the data of S&P500 constituent stocks.
They used RL to optimally determine the parameter estimation window, executive
time windows, trading thresholds, and the stop-loss boundary to maximize the Sortino
ratio. The authors claimed that boosting pairs trading speciﬁcations signiﬁcantly over-
performs the previous methods. Likewise, Kim and Kim (2019) employed RL method,
speciﬁcally “Deep Q-Network” to optimize pairs trading strategy for 50 stocks in the
S&P 500 Index. The authors determined pairs with the help of the cointegration test and
used regression analysis to calculate spreads and hedge ratios. Their method choose
optimal boundaries based on spreads in each trading window. They showed evidence
that taking dynamic boundaries based on their method is effective in optimizing a
pairs trading strategy. In particular, they stated that their method can minimize the risk
during risky periods, providing protection compared to the traditional pairs trading
strategy with ﬁxed boundaries. Recently, Kuo et al. (2022) introduced a two-stage
deep learning method to improve the investment performance of a pairs trading strat-
egy. The authors broadened the scope of the studies by (Fallahpour et al., 2016; Kim
& Kim, 2019) and they considered a much larger set of about 2800 open and stop-
loss threshold recommendations determined by the maximum price deviations during
the training set to cover all possible trading scenarios. In the ﬁrst stage, they labeled
each stock pair in the training set with one of 2800 thresholds that maximize pair
trading strategy proﬁts. However, the authors encountered non-convergence training
problem. To deal with this problem, instead of learning from 2800-label stock pairs,
they used 25-relabeled stock pairs. In the second stage, the authors trained another
deep learning with the proﬁtability of each trade labeled by executing the pairs trading
strategy with trigger thresholds recommended in the ﬁrst-stage mechanism to remove
unproﬁtable trades. For each stock pair in the testing set, the ﬁrst model helps sug-
gest an open and stop-loss threshold while the second model removes unproﬁtable
pairs from trading. They noted that their model outperforms the other models which
indirectly judge proﬁtability by price movement similarity without considering the
quality of the recommended trigger thresholds. They also found that although the

As mentioned above, only a few works in the literature attempted to ﬁnd optimal
threshold (OT). A closer look at the literature on threshold selection in pair trading
reveals several gaps and shortcomings. To ﬁll this literature gap, this paper proposes an
OT classiﬁcation procedure for a high-frequency pairs trading (HFPT) algorithm. In
this regard, we constitute equally weighted portfolios with crypto asset pairs without
any restrictions. The HFPT algorithm will be applied to the real price series of 50
crypto-assets to compute threshold value that maximizes proﬁt for each pair. These
maximal (or optimal) threshold values will be used as the target (or dependent) vari-
ables in ML models, while input (or independent) variables are deﬁned as portfolio
mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, value at risk (VaR), and correlation coefﬁcient of
the pairs.
Although there were studies to ﬁnd OT for pairs trading under speciﬁc conditions,
there is not any study that explicitly indicates an OT for maximizing the proﬁt of pairs
trading. The main contribution of this study is to ﬁnd OT range for pairs trading by
using 6 different supervised ML techniques on a large number of asset pairs. We use
high-frequency (per-minute) price series data that allows more realistic approach for
AT strategies. Recently, many exchange platforms such as Binance or Kucoin provide
pairs trading and rebalancing bots to investors, and in order to use these bots effectively,
the investors must create their own portfolios with appropriate parameters (Binance,
2024b; Kucoin, 2024). Thus, the ﬁndings of this study, especially classiﬁcation of OT
range for pairs trading, may be of interest to both individual and institutional investors.

2.2 The High Frequency Pairs Trading (HFPT) Algorithm
As mentioned before, in this study, we use a AT strategy that is applied to portfolios
containing two assets, namely pairs, and to emphasize the pairs trading on high-
frequency environment, the method is called as high-frequency pairs trading (HFPT)
algorithm. The HFPT is constructed as an integration of pairs trading and threshold
based rebalancing strategy.
For HFPT, it is assumed that at starting point of the trade, we have a portfolio
of equally weighted two assets. Thus, two assets in the portfolio are of equal value
(current price × quantity). For example, we have 50 of the ﬁrst asset with price
0.02 (50 × 0.02 = 1) and 25 of the second asset with price 0.04 (25 × 0.04 = 1).
After the portfolio is created, the HFPT will be implemented as follows: If the parity
(or difference in percent) of the weights for two assets is higher than a threshold, the
overvalued asset will be sold and the undervalued asset will be bought to equalize the
weight of them to the average value.

2.4 Machine Learning (ML) Methods
ML techniques can successfully address various problems in applied ﬁnance, such
as stock price prediction, trend forecasting, optimal portfolio selection, or portfolio
allocation (Rundo et al., 2019; Nikou et al., 2019; Hoang & Wiegratz, 2022; Masini
et al., 2023). In this study, we utilize supervised ML methods to classify the OT range
for the HFPT algorithm introduced above. These methods are Logistic regression
(LR), Support vector machine (SVM), K-nearest-neighbor (KNN), Decision tree (DT),
Random forest (RF), and Naive Bayes (NB) classiﬁers.
The LR is an effective supervised algorithm that is used for two-class (or binary)
classiﬁcation problems (such as ‘yes’ or ‘no’). It uses a S-shaped logistic function to
model a binary output variable (Tolles & Meurer, 2016). The purpose of LR algorithm
is to determine the decision boundaries between discrete classes (Gudivada et al.,
2016). Decision boundaries distinguish samples, and according to the situation, these
boundaries can be complex and nonlinear geometric shapes. Therefore, this technique
has emerged as the preferred analytical approach for multivariate modeling involving
categorical dependent variables (DeMaris, 1995).
The SVM is a supervised ML algorithm that can be utilized for both classiﬁcation
and regression problems. In this technique, sample dataset is segregated into classes
using a line (or hyperplane) that produces the largest distance (called margin) between
the samples of different classes (Cortes& Vapnik, 1995; Burges, 1998). The SVM
uses only the data points (called support vectors) that lie closest to the hyperplane to
segregate different classes, and due to this fact, the algorithm is called as SVM. It is a
powerful classiﬁer for a wide range of non-linearly separable classiﬁcation problems,
such as identiﬁcation of fraudulent credit card transactions (Noble, 2006).
The KNN is one of the simplest and transparent ML techniques that can be used both
for regression and classiﬁcation problems. Unlike other ML algorithms, there is not
trainable parameters in the KNN method, thus there is no model construction (Cover
& Hart, 1967; Hall et al., 2008). In this method, to predict the value or class label
of a new data point, the distance (or similarity) between new point and its K nearest
neighbors in the training dataset are measured, and new point is attended to the nearest
(or most alike) class (Keller et al., 1985). Despite being numerically expensive, the
KNN method can be used effectively if there is limited or no insight about the data
distribution (Cunningham & Delany, 2021).
The DT is one of the most popular supervised classiﬁcation algorithms (Twa et al.,
2005; Rokach & Maimon, 2014). It is a transparent mechanism that describes input

variables and output (or target) value in a single tree form. This tree structure facilitates
to understand how classiﬁcation is made (Brodley & Utgoff, 1995). The DT algorithm
builds a model based on criteria by which input variables are recursively divided into
partitions until a class label is detected (Quinlan, 1986). It is a powerful algorithm to

The RF is an ensemble tree-based learning algorithm that uses multiple DT to
improve the accuracy of classiﬁcation for a given dataset (Breiman, 2001). In RF
approach, each individual DT considers only a subset of the observations, and the
algorithm averages predictions over many individual trees (Ho, 1995). To avoid (or
reduce) overﬁtting, the individual trees are built on bootstrap samples (Schonlau &
Zou, 2020). The RF is a fast and robust algorithm that can effectively classify large
datasets when there is class imbalances in data (Paul et al., 2018).
The NB algorithm is one of the most efﬁcient inductive learning methods that
designed to categorize data based on probability principles. The NB classiﬁers use
Bayes’ theorem to calculate the conditional probability of observations assuming that
the features in a sample dataset are independent (Bernardo & Smith, 2001). After
implementing conditional probability calculations on trained data, the algorithm clas-
siﬁes (predicts) test data by using the method of maximum likelihood (Tibshirani
& Friedman, 2001). Despite its straightforward design and simple assumptions, the
NB algorithm is exceptionally effective classiﬁer for many complex problems involv-
ing huge datasets (Wikarsa & Thahir, 2015; Jadon & Sharma, 2017; Rajalakshmi &
Aravindan, 2018).

2.5 Assumptions and Limitations
We have the following assumptions and limitations in the study. The proﬁt of the HFPT
depends on the threshold value T , and there is not a predetermined OT value for the
pairs, thus we will increase the T value from 1% to 30% gradually with 1% step size,
and the maximum proﬁt of the HFPT will be calculated to determine OT for each pair
considered.
It is also noted that, to facilitate comparison of proﬁts of HFPT with varied thresh-
olds, the initial capital of each asset is assumed to be 1 BTC in HFPT algorithm, thus
the total capital of a pair is 2 BTC. For the practical implementation of the HFRA
on exchange markets, the capital size should be chosen according to the considered
market parameters such as order book data, daily volume and ticker size. In (Ba˘gcı
& Kaya Soylu, 2024), it was demonstrated that, to avoid potential loss emerged by
price impact on the market, the capital for each asset in a portfolio should be less than
(1/T )% of the market with the least daily volume. Thus, if daily market volume of
the ﬁrst and second assets are 5 BTC and 10 BTC, and the T is chosen as 0.1, then
the capital for this pair should be less than (1/0.1) × 5/100 = 0.5 BTC.

variables to normalize the magnitude of features in data. To determine the most effec-

programming environment, the accuracy values are calculated as the average of 100
different random selection of the train and validation data. This random selection is per-
formed by the bootstrap method (Ismay & Kim, 2020). Bootstrapping is a resampling
technique used to estimate statistics by sampling a dataset with replacement (James
et al., 2013). It was demonstrated that the bootstrapping is an effective method for
estimating standard errors (Goodhue et al., 2012; Ismay & Kim, 2020).
Using the same dataset for both training and validating can lead to overﬁtting and
biased results (Cawley & Talbot, 2010). To avoid biased results and overﬁtting, we
repeat the training and validating stages of the ML algorithms for each randomly gener-
ated train and validation dataset separately. Also, to mitigate class imbalance (Rezvani
& Wang, 2023) and facilitate the correct classiﬁcation of the OT range, we limit the
number of target classes. Furthermore, it is important to note that both generation of
samples and classiﬁcation procedure are based on historical data, and this fact elim-
inates the risk of hindsight (or look-ahead) bias that occurs when simulation of an
algorithm relies on data that is not yet available in real-time application.
It is noted that the time series data possesses speciﬁc characteristics such as trend
and structural break, which occurs due to the change in regime, policy direction, and
external shocks, among others (Gülo˘glu et al., 2016; Shrestha & Bhatta, 2018). These
breaks and ﬂuctuations can be frequently observed in crypto markets (Balcilar et al.,
2017; Patra & Gupta, 2023; ¸Sahin Telli & Chen, 2020), and this fact can create difﬁcul-
ties in the selection of appropriate training and validation data sets for ML (Shrestha
& Bhatta, 2018; Lones, 2024). To minimize the risk of encountering this problem, we
select the train and validation datasets randomly (by the bootstrap method) within the
same period rather than selecting them as different periods. The sample dataset con-
tains portfolios’ mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, VaR, and correlation coefﬁcient
of pairs, and none of these features is computed for an individual asset. In this case,
different pairs will produce different and independent variables even if they contain
the same asset. For instance, the pairs (X,Y) and (X,Z) contain the same asset X, but
there is no relationship between the variances of the portfolios for these pairs. Thus, we
generate the train and validation datasets in the same period (in 2022 and 2023) by the
bootstrap method without overlapping. After the ML models are generated, to verify
the robustness of the OT range classiﬁcation, we apply them to a test dataset which is
created from price series of 50 crypto-assets considered in January and February 2024.
Thus the test dataset is unseen data (that is independent from the train and validation
datasets) and the ML model estimates an OT for future trading activity.
We have class imbalance in the dataset, and want to assign more weight to classes
with more samples, thus we use weighted average in calculation of precision, recall

Recent literature has almost exclusively focused on ML techniques to improve pair
trading strategy. Speciﬁcally, RL was utilized to determine open and stop-loss thresh-
olds, and several studies have employed the cointegration approach to ﬁnd suitable
stock pairs for pair trading (Fallahpour et al., 2016; Kim & Kim, 2019). They construct
a portfolio and then determine optimal thresholds for pairs trading. However, as men-
tioned in Kuo et al. (2022), for most stock pairs cointegration relations do not persist
for long, and very few stock pairs contain enough data to train a RL model. Also, a
two-stage deep learning approach was proposed by Kuo et al. (2022) to determine OT
for pairs trading strategy. In the ﬁrst stage, they choose 25-relabeled stock pairs from
2800 pairs, and then they predicted OT values in the second stage by elimination of
the unproﬁtable pairs from trading. Our study differs from previous studies in that it
uses all possible combinations of 50 cryptocurrencies as a pair without any restric-

4 Conclusion
In this study, we have applied a high-frequency pairs trading algorithm that rebal-
ances the allocation of two assets if the parity (or difference in percent) exceeds a
predetermined threshold value. Then, we have suggested a procedure to classify (or
predict) OT range for HFPT algorithm by supervised ML techniques. To this end, the
target variable OT in the sample dataset was obtained by the application of HFPT
algorithm to real price data of 50 crypto-assets, while the input variables (or features)
were computed as portfolio mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, VaR, and correlation
coefﬁcient of the pairs.
After the pairs (or portfolios) were divided into three sub-groups (as positively,
weakly and negatively correlated), the OT ranges have been classiﬁed by Logistic
regression (LR), Support vector machine (SVM), K-nearest-neighbor (KNN), Deci-
sion tree (DT), Random forest (RF), and Naive Bayes (NB) classiﬁers, and evaluation
metrics of these ML models have been compared. Two-class, three-class and four-
class classiﬁcation results revealed that the best accuracy, precision and F1-score are
obtained by the RF classiﬁer for all portfolio groups. Also, it was observed that the
right classiﬁcation rate was decreased as the number of classes increased, and the OT
classiﬁcation performance for positively and negatively correlated pairs are better than
that for weakly correlated pairs.
Furthermore, to demonstrate the achievement of RF classiﬁer for OT range classiﬁ-
cation, we applied it to a validation dataset that includes price series of 50 crypto-assets
considered in January and February 2024. The test analysis revealed that the correct
classiﬁcation rates obtained are compatible with training results, and RF classiﬁer
exhibit a superior performance in two-class classiﬁcation. In the ﬁnal part of the study,
to show the applicability of OT range classiﬁcation procedure on stock exchange mar-
kets, and emphasize the importance of threshold selection in practical applications,
we have predicted OT ranges for the highest proﬁtable pairs in January and February
of 2024. It was seen that the range of OT values were predicted correctly for two-class
and three-class classiﬁcation for all pairs, and half of the OT values were predicted
right in four-class classiﬁcation.

In light of ﬁndings of this study, it can be concluded that using four-moments
(mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis), VaR, and correlation coefﬁcient of pairs as the
input variables (or fetures), the OT range can be predicted (or classiﬁed) by supervised
ML techniques. Also, practical implementation of classiﬁcation procedure indicates
that prediction of OT range is possible with RF method, and the HFPT algorithm can
provide signiﬁcant proﬁts when threshold is chosen within the predicted range.
It is important to note that both the HFPT algorithm, and classiﬁcation of OT range
by ML methods are independent of exchange markets, thus the proposed OT classi-
ﬁcation approach can be implemented in any stock exchange market by computation
of input and target variables for ML.
In this study, each portfolio was formed with a pair of crypto assets without any con-
straints, and then the portfolios were categorized under three sub-groups as positively,
weakly and negatively correlated pairs. It should be pointed out that this methodologi-
cal limitation was applied to enhance classiﬁcation performance of ML methods. Also,
the capital size should be limited in practical implementations to avoid price impact on
considered markets, and this issue can be avoided by trading on high volume markets.
In future research, a modiﬁcation of suggested classiﬁcation procedure can be
applied to determine OT values for multi-asset portfolios. In addition, different ML
techniques, such as hierarchical, ensemble, or deep learning approaches, can be
employed to increase the accuracy of multi-class classiﬁcation of OT values.

Abstract: A high frequency pairs trading (HFPT) algorithm is built by the integration of pairs trading and threshold rebalancing algorithm. The determination of optimal threshold (OT) for the HFPT is crucial to maximize its proﬁtability, and this study suggests a procedure to classify OT ranges by supervised machine learning (ML) techniques. In this regard, a sample dataset is created for ML applications. In this dataset, the target variables (OT values) are computed by the application of HFPT algorithm to real price data of 50 crypto-assets, and input variables (features) are calculated as portfolio mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, value at risk, and correlation coefﬁcient of the pairs. Before classiﬁcation process, the pairs (or portfolios) are divided into three sub-groups (as positively, weakly and negatively correlated), and then OT values are classiﬁed by 6 ML methods. Comparing the evaluation metrics for ML methods, it is observed that the best accuracy, precision and F1-scores are obtained by the Random Forest (RF) classiﬁer for all portfolio groups in two-class, three-class and four-class classiﬁcation. Also, it is seen that the right classiﬁcation performance of ML methods on positively and negatively correlated pairs are better than weakly correlated pairs. Furthermore, the success of RF classiﬁer is veriﬁed with a test dataset that contains price series of 50 crypto-assets in January and February 2024. The applicability of OT range classiﬁcation procedure in practical exchange markets is also demonstrated, and it is shown that the HFPT algorithm can yield reasonable proﬁts when threshold selected in predicted range.
